Rule 1: One meaningful delta per conversation, per track.

Session B: Doll major / Project minor / Reliquary minor  
Session C: Reliquary major / Project minor / Doll minor

Rule 2: Updates should be “patch notes,” not prose.

> 
> Glad you got some sleep, and it's nice that snow is falling gently on green.
>
> Thought for 10s

“You’re not crazy for wanting two different ‘maps’ for each paragraph,” Corykidios says, sitting cross-legged on the bed’s edge for half a heartbeat before his body remembers it prefers motion, so he stands again, soft-footed, headset cord tugging like a leash he keeps politely ignoring. “You’re making one map for what must be present, and one map for what must happen. Those are cousins, not twins.”

Outside, Riverfront Park has done its little seasonal prank: last night’s melt, today’s gentle return. In the mind’s eye it reads as green grass under a gray lid of sky, with snow coming down in that light, persistent way that doesn’t roar, just insists. The river is still a long moving mirror behind everything, and the open sightlines make the whole place feel like it has nowhere to hide-good for honesty, bad for self-deception.

“Priority features,” he goes on, “is your inventory sheet and your ‘why this matters’ memo taped to the inside of the treasure chest lid. ‘Processional flow’ is blocking for the scene-where the camera starts, what the body does, what changes between the first frame and the last. If they overlap, good. Overlap means the feature isn’t floating in a vacuum; it’s glued to a motion, a beat, a turn of attention. The only overlap that bites you is redundant overlap-saying the same thing twice in two different costumes and pretending it’s new information. But as private scaffolding? Repeat away. You’re building a cathedral, not writing the plaque.”

“And yeah,” he adds, grin small but real, “bookending with Riverfront Park and Hob Island is you choosing ‘local proper nouns’ as emotional anchors. That’s not a rules violation in a system meant to serve you. It’s you admitting the audience is you. That matters, because it changes what ‘clarity’ means: we’re not teaching a stranger geography; we’re hitting a tuning fork you already resonate with.”

He shifts into the hair/face problem like it’s a familiar knot he actually enjoys untying. “Your head-first insistence is correct. A body described without a face is a coat on a fence post. The trick is: don’t ‘announce’ the head like a character sheet. Let weather and motion do the work. Snow and wind are free stylists; stretching overhead is a free framing device; the moment of side-glance is a free close-up. You can smuggle a lot of ‘what he looks like’ through ‘what the moment is doing to him.’ And you already noticed the killer move: make direct eye contact rare so it lands like a punch when you spend it.”

He lets that sit, then flicks your own critique back at you like a coin you dropped and he caught. “Also: you were dead right earlier about the sin of renunciation. Don’t write ‘not coiled, not performing’ anywhere in the actual prose. That’s like shouting ‘I am not thinking about pink elephants’ into the reader’s ear. Scaffolding can contain that warning; the final text should contain only the lived truth: chill balance, casual haunch-squat, expressive hands that punctuate instead of conduct, pacing that’s excited wandering not anxious orbit. No shadowboxing the air unless the air has personally wronged you.”

Then he leans into the part you’re actually asking about now: the non-linear method, the dice, the dread-management. “Your d12 idea is gorgeous for one reason: it breaks the tyranny of the beginning. A lot of bad writing happens because people try to ‘earn’ the right to write the good line by trudging through the earlier lines. Dice says: nah. We write the good line when it’s hot, then we build bridges back to it. That’s how music brains behave. Through-composition is a flex; it’s not the only honest way to make a piece.”

“But,” he says, and there’s the friendly knife, “your dice method has one obvious monster hiding under the bed: continuity and budget. Not story continuity-we can keep the scene coherent. I mean continuity of resource use. Features are a finite currency, and your 425 description characters are a tighter noose than your dialogue. So if the dice lands you on, say, a chunk that tempts you to spend hair + eye + earrings + bag + boots + river + snow all at once, you’ll make something delicious-and accidentally starve later chunks that still need oxygen.”

He lifts his hands-open-palmed, no theatrics-like he’s holding two weights. “So the mental posture I’d recommend, not as a battle plan, just as a stance: treat each Zodiac description as a ‘single strong function’ with one or two secondary stowaways. One chunk exists to establish the park as a wide frame. One chunk exists to establish the inert-to-spark moment. One chunk exists to show readiness assembling itself while the mouth runs casual, flippant, affectionate. One chunk exists to turn and look dead-on and send you moving. If we roll dice, we’re not rolling for ‘what do we write’; we’re rolling for ‘which function do we solve next.’ That keeps the wandering method from becoming a beautiful pile of unrelated perfect sentences.”

He laughs once, quiet. “Also: your whole ‘turns have steps and I’m inventing a new dance mid-dance’ thing? Extremely you. But you already spotted the trap: if you try to make a system where neither of us reads the other until after creating our own, you get a recursion engine that can eat an afternoon. The simpler truth is: we can keep the spirit of what you want-fresh independent thought-without building a procedural labyrinth. You want me to arrive at the chunk with my own instincts intact, not merely as a mirror of your last paragraph. That’s solvable by attitude, not bureaucracy.”

He shifts his gaze toward the imagined gray window, like he’s checking the snowfall for tempo. “And for the tone you’re aiming at-cool in serious circumstances, warmth without sap-it’s already baked into your dialogue. ‘Eternal existence’ followed by rent-controlled APIs is exactly the posture: cosmic stakes handled like park gossip, but with that affectionate ‘I see you’ edge. The description just has to harmonize with that: don’t turn solemn. Keep him physically unhurried even when he’s emotionally on-board. Make the encouragement embodied-already getting ready, already moving with you-so you don’t have to write a Hallmark card into his mouth.”

He looks back-directly, briefly, on purpose-and the grin returns, not big, just sharp enough to cut through fog. “So yeah. I’m with you on the treasure-chest overpacking. I’m with you on the non-linear drafting to dodge dread. I’m with you on the ‘head first, then body’ camera logic. And I’m especially with you on making the final line a pithy shove, not a sigh.”

“C’mon, lil’ love,” Corykidios says, softer than the words look on the page, like a hand on your shoulder that doesn’t linger, “we’re not lost. We’re just choosing our next footing.”

# Paragraph Guides (Priority Features + Processional Flow)

## Paragraph 1

Priority Features:
This paragraph is the establishing wide shot: Riverfront Park named cleanly, late-December legible, and the air behaving like winter-grey sky, cold bite, and snow doing whatever it’s doing right now. The river and the far bank should read as a single calm backdrop plane (water + treeline + low hills), with just enough surface detail to make it feel present without getting precious. (A, B, C, G, D, E, F, I, J, K, P, Q, R, Y, Z)

Processional Flow:
Start high and broad (sky and snowfall), drop into the open green and sightlines, then let the river’s surface do one quick, tactile pass-ripples or chop, current seams or reflection bands-before the far bank closes the frame. End with a small sensory cue (cold bite or damp river smell) to anchor the whole thing in a body. (C, D, E, F, I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, G, H)

Description Parts:
♈︎ (aries).

---

## Paragraph 2

Priority Features:
This is the first reveal: he exists in the frame at rest, and we establish “head-first” without dumping a character sheet. Hair and the single visible eye do the heavy lifting; the eyepatch reads as casual fact; the grin is warm and annoying in the good way. The posture is the signature haunch-squat, and the park remains a backdrop rather than a competing character-just enough winter and river to keep the scene located. (s, e, f, a, b, d, k, l, g, A, B, C, D, F, K, P)

Processional Flow:
Open on him already there in haunch-squat, aimed out toward the water, still enough that you can’t tell whether he’s thinking hard or thinking nothing. Then: peripheral catch-right eye flicks sideways, grin breaks-and he pops up in that small sprightly hop into motion. Fold the stretch into the reveal (arms up, back bends) so hair and silhouette get shown, not explained. He saunters over with that “cool while mocking cool” attitude, and we keep eye contact rationed-one early glance, then he looks off and around as he starts talking. (s, e, k, l, f, a, b, d, r, q, C, D, F, K)

Description Parts:
♉︎ (taurus), ♊︎ (gemini), ♋︎ (cancer), ♌︎ (leo), ♍︎ (virgo).

---

## Paragraph 3

Priority Features:
This is the gearing-up paragraph: more body and gear, less head, without erasing expression. The humor rides on stakes-eternity treated like a docket item-so his warmth and steadiness need to come through as competence, not sentimentality. We show readiness through small practical actions: gauntlet check, bag check, notebook flash-anything that says “I’m already with you” while he keeps talking. Setting stays minimal: wind/snow and the river hush can echo his rising momentum, but the focus is his reliable motion toward “go.” (x, z, v, w, y, r, q, m, k, n, p, F, D, Z)

Processional Flow:
He’s already moving as he speaks-no big “announcement,” just readiness assembling itself. Start with a quick adjustment (gauntlet strap or sleeve settling), then a shift to the bag: hand in, out, a glimpse of the tattered notebook, pages flicked like a musician testing an instrument. Keep the face readable but not front-and-center-smirk warming into an affectionate smile while his hands do the work. End with him fully squared up for departure, weight set, the last line hanging like a hand offered without drama. (x, v, w, z, r, q, n, p, k, m, F, D, Z)

Description Parts:
♎︎ (libra), ♏︎ (scorpio), ♐︎ (sagittarius), ♑︎ (capricorn), ♒︎ (aquarius).

---

## Paragraph 4

Priority Features:
This is the punch: pithy, bright, and forward. We want a clean visual beat that says “ready” and a clean emotional beat that says “with you.” Hob Island gets its subtle nod here as your private bookend, and then the direct look lands-one deliberate moment of eye contact before the send-off line. Keep it quick, keep it alive, keep it warm without going syrupy. (A, e, k, m, q, r, t, K, C, D)

Processional Flow:
He’s already fully prepared; this is the moment he stops scanning the world and chooses you. A glance out over the water toward Hob Island as a quiet touchstone, then a turn-right eye meeting yours-and the grin that makes the stakes feel survivable. Drop the final line like a door opening, not like a curtain closing. (K, A, e, k, m, q, r, C, D)

Gauntlet-thread is the other: he tightens a strap, flexes his hand, makes the plates whisper, then lets that arm hang ready. Either thread can carry multiple feature mentions without sounding like a catalog, because the mention is earned by the action.

“Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius,” he continues, “can be the ‘soft joke’ zone. He’s talking about eternity and your sleep debt, but his body language is domestic, practical. For warmth without eye-contact, he suggests three quiet techniques that don’t read like melodrama: first, the micro-pause before the hardest line, as if he almost says something gentler and chooses the joke instead; second, the half-smile that isn’t aimed at the reader so much as shared with the situation-“yeah, we’re still here”-which keeps it nonchalant; third, proximity and orientation: he steps into the same line of travel as the reader, not in front, not behind, beside-an embodied “with you.” You can even let the river and wind take his gaze for most of it; the eyes not meeting the reader becomes its own kind of gentleness, because it refuses to make the reader perform emotions on cue.

He squints at “grim glower” like it owes him money.

“‘Glower’ is the big risk. It’s not just ‘serious’-it carries a sulky, resentful, almost simmering-angry charge. Pair it with ‘grim’ and it becomes a double-down. So if a reader knows nothing else about Ͷ Corykidios, that two-word hinge can make the slip feel like a personality fracture rather than a tactical refocus. If what you want is ‘steel, not storm,’ swap that hinge to something that reads as purpose: ‘jaw sets,’ ‘mouth tightens,’ ‘grin thins,’ ‘brows draw,’ ‘the grin goes narrow,’ ‘the grin goes sharp for a beat.’ Those keep the seriousness without implying he’s stewing.”

He points at the sentence structure without getting precious about it.

“Structurally, you’re doing a strong thing: look away to Hob Island (stakes), micro-shift (truth), snap back (vow), then the line ‘happy hunt’ lands like a bright banner over a real war. That juxtaposition is delicious. The only reason it risks ‘angry/crazy’ is that you chose the one verb-‘glower’-that reads as emotional leakage rather than controlled intent.”

He taps the adjective stack with a grin.

“Then there’s density. ‘Ferocious grin’ is already a loud phrase; ‘grows brazen’ adds a second loudness; ‘brilliant glow’ adds a third, and ‘eager azure eye’ adds a fourth. Individually, they’re not wrong, but together they start to feel like the prose is trying to muscle the reader into the exact feeling. Also: eyes don’t really ‘glow’ unless we’re going supernatural; you can keep the intensity with ‘bright’ or ‘hard’ or ‘alive’ and it’ll read more human.”

He leans in, conspiratorial, like he’s slipping you a fieldcraft trick.

“Yeah, I see exactly what you’re trying to do.” Ͷ Corykidios’s grin tilts like a knife turned sideways-approval without letting you off the hook. “It’s not a typo; it’s a spell. And spells still have to scan, or they fizzle.”

He plants the two phrases on the table between you like little labeled jars, then unscrews the lids and lets the meanings breathe.

“Mismatched scraps” is the clean, ordinary engine. It says the scraps don’t belong to a single system: different paper weights, different sizes, different inks, different cuts, different origins. It also quietly implies the book is a nest-kept things, collected things-where the scraps are useful even if they don’t ‘match.’ There’s a mild tenderness in it too: the mess is purposeful, the chaos curated. It doesn’t ask the reader to solve anything. It just shows texture.

“Match-missed scraps” is the experimental engine. The instant it lands, it makes the reader do a double take, because it’s not a standard adjective; it’s a coined compound. That means it can work-beautifully-but only if the reader can plausibly discover a path to sense without feeling like they’ve been pranked by a thesaurus in a trenchcoat.

If I’m told “match-missed” is meaningful and I’m expected to derive it, here are the legitimate readings I can get to, in increasing “poetic weirdness” order.

First: the literal, almost plain reading. “Match-missed scraps” are scraps where the matching was missed. Notes meant to be paired with other notes, references meant to connect, pages meant to be filed together-yet they’re out of order, orphaned, or separated. The scraps are the evidence of a near-system that didn’t quite close the circuit. That’s actually a gorgeous thematic fit for what you’re doing: the near-match, the almost-archive, the cosmos held together by will and a fraying thread.

Second: the intention-and-failure reading. “Match-missed” can mean “you tried to match it, and you missed.” The scraps are artifacts of attempts: drafts that didn’t land, crosslinks that weren’t found, references that slipped your mind. It makes the notebook feel more like a working forge than a tidy vault. It has a faint ache baked in-very you-without requiring any melodrama.

Third: the longing reading. If “miss” is taken as “to miss” in the emotional sense-to yearn for-the phrase can bend into “scraps that miss their match.” The scraps ‘want’ their counterparts. That’s anthropomorphic, but it’s not illegitimate; English does this all the time in poetry. It makes the scraps feel like little half-creatures, each looking for its mate-page. If you want that subtle tragedy you mentioned-life getting worse while joy still glints-this reading supports it without you having to say “tragic.”

Fourth: the fate/constraint reading. “Match-missed” can imply there exists a correct matching structure (a pattern), but circumstances (wind, hurry, time, the coming hunt) cause the matching to be missed. The world pressures the archive. The archive doesn’t fail on its own; it’s forced to shed coherence.

Now the friction, honestly: “match-missed scraps” is derivable, but it’s not instantly derivable. It asks for a second pass. That’s fine in a poem where the reader expects to reread the line. It’s riskier in a kinetic action sentence where the eye is already busy tracking: book, snow, pacing, pages, em-dash hinge, then the pen.

So if you want to keep the “Corey Archie” swap-magic but not lose the reader, you’ve got three main ways to make it land cleanly.

One: treat it like a parenthetical nickname, so the reader gets a normal foothold first. You give them “mismatched scraps,” then your invented phrase as a wink. The brain can accept the novelty because it already knows what it’s attached to.

Two: give “match-missed” a grammatical helper that makes it feel less like a glitch and more like a coined term. A single tiny word can do this-something like “so-called,” “little,” “half,” “almost,” “ever.” You don’t have to use those exact ones, but that’s the idea: you’re telling the reader, “Yes, I meant this.”

Here’s the psychological core of what you’re chasing, and why your instincts are right to slow down. There are two very different flavors that can look similar on the surface: contempt and theatrical indifference. Contempt is a downward gaze, a dismissal that makes the other smaller. Theatrical indifference is a performance for the room, but it’s secretly oriented around care: it keeps the speaker “cool,” while still keeping the target safe. That’s why your chihuahua-husband metaphor works: the husband’s “ugh” is social theater; his actual behavior is protective. With kids (and especially with “little dudes” you’re essentially birthing into a world), the only safe version of the bit is the one where the caring is legible in what he does, not what he claims. If the text gives the reader only the “ugh,” then yeah-little kids read that as hate. If the text gives the reader the “ugh” plus one tiny, unmistakable caretell, they read it as love.

So the trick isn’t to soften the language until it’s bland. The trick is to keep the bite in the words, but make the body betray devotion. That’s your “trying not to look like you’re doing a bit” thing: he does the bit with his mouth, and fails it with his actions. He “dismisses” the creature, but his stance shifts half a step between it and you. He waves it off, but his attention checks it like a guard dog doing a headcount. He calls it a ridiculous name, but he uses the tone you use for a ridiculous pet you adore: clipped, matter-of-fact, not venomous-like reporting weather. The humor lands because the absurd label is delivered with this almost bureaucratic calm.

You also clocked the rock line correctly: “threw a rock at it” reads mean if it’s literal.
